source.title: Time-Aware Feature Selection: Adaptive Temporal Masking for Stable Sparse Autoencoder Training

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures feature absorption in SAE representations and reports that absorption remains method-dependent, refining claims that SAE features are stable, canonical units. It also evaluates sparse-probe recovery in an LLM setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports absorption scores and sparse-probing accuracies for SAE variants. Reconstruction and sparsity metrics are not included because they do not directly measure the claim versions. Comparisons to prior work mentioned in the text are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: This is an SAE training-method paper. It proposes Adaptive Temporal Masking (ATM) and compares its absorption, reconstruction and sparse-probing scores with TopK, JumpReLU and standard SAEs on Gemma-2-2B layer 12. It uses SAEs as a tool and reports its own method's performance. It does not test whether superposition holds in toy models, whether polysemanticity comes from capacity, whether LLMs contain recoverable sparse features, or whether dictionary features are canonical units. Sparse-probe accuracy of SAE latents says nothing about superposition itself. The absorption differences across training methods bear only loosely on V5 and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it should be corrected. The authors conclude that ATM cuts absorption about 40% versus the best baseline (JumpReLU) while keeping strong reconstruction. Their conclusion also claims 'superior sparse probing accuracy'. Table 1 contradicts this: TopK (0.7698) beats ATM (0.7161). Table 1 also shows the standard SAE with better reconstruction than ATM (MSE 0.0898 vs 0.5508).
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates sparse autoencoders with adaptive temporal masking on a transformer layer; it does not reproduce the original toy-network feature-superposition setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Absorption and sparse-probing results differ across SAE methods; the e-words absorption comparison also varies by method.

fits_no_version.finding: Absorption scores vary about 20-fold across SAE training methods on the same layer: TopK 0.1402, standard SAE 0.0161, JumpReLU 0.0114, ATM 0.0068. None is zero. The SAEs differ greatly in sparsity (L0 40 to 8724 of 16384), confounding the comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How much feature absorption a dictionary shows depends on the SAE training method and sparsity regime.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to Gemma-2-2B layer 12 and 5M training tokens. The authors report running experiments on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 and say they could not evaluate larger models, deeper networks, more tokens, or systematically investigate hyperparameters. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing directly on the claim versions were left out. The paper's reconstruction, sparsity, and other downstream-task metrics were excluded because they do not directly measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis of neurons.
All: no comparison of neuron-basis and dictionary representations, and no evidence that features are distributed across neurons.
Completeness, stability across seeds, and canonicity are not measured. Absorption is reported only as a metric for ranking training methods.

record.verdict_notes: Small workshop study: one model, one layer, 5M training tokens, one GPU, no uncertainty estimates. ATM's L0 of 3280 exceeds the hidden dimension of 2304, so its dictionary is not sparse in the usual sense, and the low absorption may reflect this. The setup describes EMA beta as 0.9 in Methods and 0.99 in Experiments, an inconsistency. The reader's V4 and V5 labels were removed because the rows are method comparisons that cannot bear on those versions.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise through causes other than capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE sparse-probe recovery in one model and layer, not whether features are distributed across many neurons.
It measures absorption and probe performance, but not whether SAE features are complete, canonical, stable across seeds, or stable across checkpoints.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
